The map's label for the patchwork of Muslim and Hindu ruled states across northern and central India between about 1530 and 1650, outside the firm core of the big empires.

In 1530 Babur had just died and the Mughal hold was weak. The Afghan Sher Shah Suri drove out Babur's son Humayun in 1540, and the Mughals came back only in 1555. Around and between them were many smaller powers:

  • Rajput kingdoms in Rajputana, where Mewar under Maharana Pratap resisted the Mughals;
  • Gond kingdoms in the central forests, where queen Rani Durgavati died fighting a Mughal army in 1564;
  • Afghan chiefs and sultanates in the north and east;
  • the Ahom kingdom of Assam, which beat back Mughal invasions.

Akbar and his heirs drew many of these into the Mughal Empire by war and by marriage alliances, but local rulers kept much of their power.
sum: The map's label for the patchwork of Muslim and Hindu ruled states across northern and central India between about 1530 and 1650, outside the firm core of the big empires.
